cards.title: Benefit-Driven CTA Buttons for Product Pages
cards.summary: Make the primary product-page CTA visually dominant and frame the click around the shopper’s desired outcome rather than a generic action.
cards.use_when: Designing the main add-to-cart, bundle-selection, or campaign-page CTA for a physical product.
steps: Identify the shopper’s immediate desired outcome after evaluating the product: choose a routine, claim the bundle saving, find their fit, or start using the product. Use that benefit in nearby headline and supporting copy rather than relying solely on a generic button label.

Keep the transactional button clear where platform conventions require it, such as “Add to cart,” but make the surrounding CTA unit benefit-led. For example, a bundle selector could lead with “Build your 30-day routine and save” above the add-to-cart button.

Make the primary button physically prominent with generous padding, strong contrast, and a clear visual priority on desktop and mobile. The source’s examples also use all-caps button labels, though this is a stylistic choice rather than a requirement.
Keep the promise consistent from acquisition creative through the product page and cart. A shopper who clicked for a stated benefit should see that same benefit reinforced at the purchase action.
Avoid vague adjacent copy such as “Learn more” when the shopper is ready to select a product or bundle.
caveats: The source’s observations come from client work rather than a controlled universal benchmark. Test benefit framing, button styling, and mobile placement with your own traffic.
Do not imply outcomes the product cannot substantiate.

cards.title: Match the Product-Page Hero to Traffic Awareness
cards.summary: Lead with product selection for high-intent visitors, but lead with the problem, mechanism, and product relevance when campaign traffic is less aware.
cards.use_when: Choosing the above-the-fold structure for a PDP, collection landing page, or advertorial-to-product journey based on acquisition source and shopper intent.
steps: Segment the intended traffic by awareness. Visitors arriving from branded search, a category search, or a direct product query are typically closer to choosing a solution; show the product, key benefit, price or bundle options, CTA, and trust cues immediately.

For social-ad or other interruption traffic, do not assume visitors understand the product category or why it matters. Start with a concise problem or desired outcome, explain the product’s relevant mechanism or use case honestly, then introduce selection options.

For high-intent product traffic, make the hero conversion unit dense but readable: benefit-led headline, product imagery, three to four expectation-setting bullets, bundle or variant choice, a prominent add-to-cart CTA, and risk-reduction or proof nearby.
For lower-awareness traffic, put education before demanding a choice. Use real customer proof, factual product explanation, and a clear bridge to the PDP or product selector.
Review results by traffic source rather than applying one hero to every visitor.
caveats: Awareness is a planning heuristic, not a substitute for analytics. Validate with product-page engagement, add-to-cart rate, and purchase conversion by source.
Education must not make unsupported scientific, health, or root-cause claims.

cards.title: Use Pain–Agitate–Solution Ethically on Product Campaign Pages
cards.summary: For problem-aware shoppers, name the recognizable frustration, acknowledge failed alternatives, and present the product as a credible next step without exaggeration.
cards.use_when: Building a campaign landing page or advertorial-to-product journey for shoppers who recognize a problem but do not yet know which product category or brand to choose.
steps: State the exact, customer-researched frustration in language shoppers use. The goal is recognition: the visitor should understand that the page addresses their situation.

Describe the practical cost of leaving that problem unresolved or cycling through inadequate alternatives. Keep this grounded in real use experience; do not manufacture fear, diagnosis, urgency, or certainty.

Introduce the product as the relevant solution and explain why its format, ingredients, materials, compatibility, or routine addresses the stated need. Pair the claim with a CTA to choose a variant, bundle, or product.
Place this sequence close below the hero when traffic is problem-aware and needs education before shopping. For solution-aware traffic, shorten it or move it below early proof and product selection.
Put a purchase path immediately after the solution: product choice, bundle savings, real reviews, and any valid guarantee or returns information.
caveats: The source varies placement and length by audience; this is not a fixed page order.
Do not convert a product benefit into a medical diagnosis, guaranteed result, or unsupported comparative claim.

cards.title: Build Benefit-First Product Value Propositions
cards.summary: Translate product features into shopper outcomes by asking what each feature enables, then make the resulting benefit the section headline.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP benefit blocks, collection-page merchandising, product bundle descriptions, or campaign landing-page sections.
steps: List every genuine selling point: material, formulation, manufacturing process, included accessory, replenishment format, service policy, product testing, or bundle component.

For each point, ask “so that what?” until you reach the shopper-relevant consequence. A feature such as clear replenishment guidance might become a benefit such as making it easier to maintain a routine; a bundle may become fewer decisions and visible savings.
Use the benefit, rather than the feature label, as the section headline. Put supporting feature detail beneath it for shoppers who want validation.

Create enough distinct value-proposition sections to resolve the major reasons to choose the product. The source suggests three to four as a bare minimum and eight to ten for more complex offers; use fewer when the product genuinely has fewer decision factors.
Interleave authentic social proof or other evidence between major value propositions so claims are not presented as brand assertions alone.
Avoid generic headers such as “Why us,” “Our products,” or “What makes us different” unless the headline itself states the customer payoff.
caveats: The source’s reported lift from combining value propositions and social proof was a single client example with multiple changes, not proof that a specific section count will increase sales.
Only claim benefits supported by the product and available evidence.

cards.title: Write PDP Headlines for Scanners
cards.summary: Assume many shoppers scan headings rather than read every paragraph, so every heading should communicate a standalone product benefit or decision aid.
cards.use_when: Writing product-page headings, campaign-page section titles, bundle descriptions, comparison blocks, and testimonial summaries.
steps: Audit every heading without its body copy. A shopper should still understand the key benefit, use case, or proof point from the heading alone.

Replace generic labels with benefit-led statements. Instead of “Ingredients,” state the relevant shopper implication, then provide the ingredient details beneath it; instead of “Reviews,” summarize the genuine theme of the proof.

Use a clear hierarchy: the hero claim first, then the most important decision information, followed by supporting details. Use type size, weight, and color contrast to distinguish headings from body copy.
Keep body copy available for substantiation and product specifics, but do not force shoppers to read it to understand why a section matters.
Apply the same scanning discipline to review cards: a short, accurate summary heading can surface the relevant usage outcome, while the full verified review remains available below.
caveats: The source cites a general rule of thumb that people read only a small portion of page content; treat it as a rationale for clear information design, not a precise measurement of your traffic.
Do not edit testimonial headings in a way that changes what the reviewer actually said.

cards.title: Create Scannable, Verifiable Social Proof
cards.summary: Use real reviews and customer stories in visible, varied formats, with accurate source attribution and summaries that let shoppers grasp the proof quickly.
cards.use_when: Adding reviews, UGC, case stories, or customer proof to a PDP, product landing page, bundle page, or cart-adjacent offer.
steps: Select genuine proof that answers actual purchase objections: product fit, ease of use, quality, delivery experience, repeat purchase, or the relevant outcome of use.
Show the review source where applicable, such as a verified review platform or identifiable first-party review system, so shoppers can assess credibility. Do not add attribution that is not real.
Give each review a concise heading that accurately captures its central point, allowing scanners to understand the proof before reading the full text or watching a video.

Mix formats where assets are authentic: text reviews, customer video, product-in-use imagery, result statistics with clear context, or a customer story. Use each format to answer a different uncertainty rather than repeating the same claim.

Keep important proof open and accessible on mobile. The source cautions that standard content carousels often receive little engagement; prioritize visible review cards before hiding core proof behind interaction.
Repeat relevant proof near major decision points, particularly product selection, bundle choice, and the final purchase prompt.
caveats: All reviews, customer imagery, results, and source labels must be authentic and accurately represented.
The source also cites a rotating image-plus-review treatment as a useful format; distinguish that deliberate proof unit from hiding an entire review section in a generic carousel.

cards.title: Use Comparison Tables to Simplify Product Choice
cards.summary: Help shoppers evaluate a product, bundle, or category alternative with a factual, scannable comparison table rather than forcing them to infer differences from prose.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a flagship product against other formats, comparing bundles, or explaining how your product differs from a conventional alternative on a PDP or landing page.
steps: Identify the few decision criteria shoppers truly use: included items, compatibility, material or ingredient attributes, maintenance, usage format, subscription flexibility, shipping terms, or price-per-use where it can be calculated honestly.
Build columns for your product or bundle and the relevant alternatives. Use checks, blanks, or other simple visual markers so differences can be grasped quickly.
Add a short explanation in the table only where a binary symbol could mislead. Complex products often need a line of context explaining what an attribute means in use.
Frame row labels around customer-relevant benefits, but substantiate them with factual attributes. The table should help shoppers choose, not merely list favorable marketing language.
Place the table after the shopper understands the product’s basic proposition, or near bundle selection when it resolves a choice between options.
Review every comparison claim for accuracy, currency, and fair characterization of alternatives.
caveats: Do not stack a comparison with unverifiable superiority claims or omit material qualifications that would change a fair interpretation.
A table cannot replace core PDP details such as ingredients, sizing, compatibility, fulfillment, or return terms.

cards.title: Show How the Product Fits Into the Customer Routine
cards.summary: Use a short three- or four-step how-it-works sequence that makes adoption feel clear and ends with the honest customer outcome.
cards.use_when: Explaining product setup, routine, replenishment, bundle usage, or a product-matching flow on a PDP or campaign landing page.
steps: Reduce the customer journey to the few actions required to get value: choose the appropriate product or bundle, receive it, use it as directed, and reach the realistic intended benefit.
Make each step concrete and operationally true. If a quiz is used, ask only questions about fit, preferences, routine, compatibility, or consumption that actually change recommendations or education.
Keep the process visually simple. The source favors three or four high-level steps because the sequence should make effort feel understandable rather than burdensome.

End with the shopper’s desired benefit, not merely the final mechanical action. For example, end on maintaining a simpler routine or using the product with confidence, provided that outcome is supported by the product’s purpose.
Place a CTA after the sequence that matches the next logical action: choose a product, view a recommended bundle, or add the selected option to cart.
Use supporting details or instructions elsewhere for customers who need deeper guidance.
caveats: Do not invent delivery timing, effortlessness, personalized recommendations, or product outcomes.
For regulated or health-adjacent products, avoid diagnosis, predictions, and claims beyond approved substantiation.

cards.title: Design Product Selection, Bundle Savings, and Add-to-Cart as One Flow
cards.summary: Put product choice near the top, calculate bundle value for the shopper, and confirm add-to-cart without disruptive page reloads.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing the purchase area of a PDP, bundle landing page, or campaign page for physical products.
steps: Place variant, size, subscription, and bundle selection high enough on the page that high-intent shoppers can act without scrolling through all education first.
For each bundle, state exactly what is included and the monetary saving versus eligible individual items. Do the calculation for the shopper rather than making them compare prices mentally.
Place relevant trust support near the selection and CTA: authentic reviews, delivery or returns information, genuine guarantees, compatibility guidance, and payment details where applicable.

Avoid a full-page refresh solely to confirm an add-to-cart action. The source considers this disruptive to conversion. Instead, use a clear current-platform-supported confirmation such as an updating cart drawer or unobtrusive cart state.
Use the cart drawer or cart surface to offer genuinely complementary cross-sells and upsells, not unrelated products. Preserve a fast, obvious route to checkout.
Measure add-to-cart rate, cart-to-checkout progression, average order value, and purchase conversion after changes; a larger cart is not valuable if checkout completion falls.
caveats: The source describes repeated A/B-testing experience but does not provide universal result figures; validate the flow on your own storefront and devices.
Verify current theme and platform behavior before implementing asynchronous cart or drawer logic.

cards.title: Structure a Complete Ecommerce Landing Page Around Decisions
cards.summary: Organize campaign and product landing pages so each section resolves the next shopper uncertainty: relevance, product choice, proof, differentiation, use, risk, and purchase.
cards.use_when: Planning a long-form product landing page, bundle campaign, or collection page that must educate and sell without becoming a generic lead-generation page.
steps: Start with a hero matched to awareness: communicate the relevant benefit, introduce the product, expose product or bundle selection for high-intent traffic, and add immediate trust cues.
Follow with the most important decision support: problem-and-solution education for lower-awareness traffic, or social proof and product comparison for solution-aware visitors.
Use benefit-first value-proposition sections to explain why the product’s attributes matter. Insert authentic proof between critical claims rather than isolating reviews in one distant block.
Add a comparison table if shoppers must choose between formats, bundles, or alternatives. Then show a short how-it-works or routine section that clarifies adoption.
Address risk with factual fulfillment, returns, compatibility, ingredient or material, and guarantee information where such a guarantee genuinely exists.

Close with a concise benefit recap, visible product selection or add-to-cart path, real proof, and expectation-setting bullets such as what is included, delivery information, and any valid returns terms.
Build FAQs from recurring pre-purchase questions in support tickets, reviews, on-site search, and customer research.
caveats: The source’s original full-page sequence was designed largely for service lead generation. Ecommerce pages should prioritize product selection, cart mechanics, and purchase objections rather than forms.
Change section order by traffic awareness and product complexity; do not treat this as a mandatory template.

cards.title: Benefit-Driven Prominent CTA Buttons
cards.summary: Make the primary CTA large, visually dominant, and phrased as the end benefit the visitor wants, not a generic action.
cards.use_when: Designing the primary call-to-action for a PDP, landing page, or quote form.
steps: Write CTA copy as the visitor's end benefit, not the mechanics. The source's examples: 'See how to end your dizziness' (their outcome, not 'learn more'), and 'Get an instant quote' instead of 'Get a free quote' — the word 'instant' implies speed.

Make the button physically large with heavy padding so it stands out on the page. The source stresses prominent size (large button, generous padding, all-caps label on the button itself) on both desktop and mobile.
Keep the benefit framing consistent across desktop and mobile versions — the source shows the same large benefit-driven CTA on both.
Avoid generic CTA labels that only describe the next click rather than what the visitor gains.
caveats: These layout observations come from the source's own client examples, not from a controlled benchmark — test against your own audience.

cards.title: Progressive Disclosure for Lead Capture Forms
cards.summary: Ask for the simplest information first, then reveal more fields only after the user starts filling the form.
cards.use_when: Reducing form abandonment on lead capture forms for B2B, services, or quote requests.
steps: Put only a single simple field (e.g., email) visible up front.
Once the user inputs that first field, open additional fields progressively.
Rely on the psychological commitment effect: once someone has filled one field they are far more likely to complete the remaining fields.
Keep the total number of fields as low as possible — the source notes you can combine first and last name into a single 'full name' field unless you have a specific reason to split them.
Separate field labels from placeholders. Placeholders-as-labels cause people (especially on mobile) to forget what they were filling in.
caveats: Progressive disclosure adds front-end logic; verify it works on mobile and does not hide required fields from users who bail early.

cards.title: Match Above-the-Fold Layout to Traffic Source and Awareness
cards.summary: Choose between a value-prop hero and a lead-capture-form hero based on whether your traffic is solution-aware or problem-aware.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a landing page should lead with a form above the fold or with education and imagery.
steps: If visitors are high-awareness and searching directly for a specific service (the source's example: 'facelift in Florida'), you can place a lead capture form above the fold to capitalize on immediate interest.

If visitors come from social ads like Facebook, they are more problem-aware or unaware — they know they have a problem but not the solution — so a form above the fold is premature. Lead with education instead.

When you do include an above-the-fold form, use the source's strongest layout: one benefit-driven headline, three to four bullets of what people can expect from filling it out, additional benefits, one large CTA button, and a risk-reduction or trust element beneath the CTA.
caveats: Awareness level is the source's heuristic; validate against your own traffic and form completion data before committing.

cards.title: Tighten Above-the-Fold Space to Fit More Information
cards.summary: Compress white space so headline, body, stats, form, and social proof all fit above the fold without overwhelming the eye.
cards.use_when: Redesigning a landing page hero or auditing a page littered with oversized white-space gaps.
steps: Identify large empty white blocks between sections. The source calls these unnecessary — information lower on the page could move higher if that space were cut.
Deliberately fit headline, body text, stats, form, social proof, phone number, and CTA button all above the fold. The source calls this intentional, with no empty white blocks.
Balance density: pack the information in while keeping it not overwhelming to the eye.
The source reports a 108% increase in qualified leads and conversions for one client after tightening the above-the-fold layout this way.
caveats: The 108% figure is a single before/after client example, not a guaranteed benchmark. Over-packing can hurt readability — test it.

cards.title: Build a Visual Hierarchy from Headline to CTA
cards.summary: Use font size, weight, color, and boldness to control the order the eye reads headline, subhead, body, and CTA.
cards.use_when: Designing or reviewing the typographic hierarchy of a landing page or PDP section.
steps: Set a clear top-to-bottom order: headline first, then next element, then body text, then subsequent paragraphs.
Establish size contrast: the source's example uses a headline around 32–33px versus body text around 16px.
Differentiate color: in the example the headline is blue and the body text is black, making the body less prominent.
Make the CTA button the most prominent interactive element — large, in the accent color, all-caps label on the button itself.
The source reports a 64% lift in conversions for a client after applying visual hierarchy above the fold.
caveats: Exact pixel values are from the source's example, not universal rules; type scales should suit your brand and readability needs.

cards.title: Pain–Agitate–Solution Section for Problem-Aware Traffic
cards.summary: Call out the exact pain, intensify it, then present your solution as the way out with a CTA.
cards.use_when: Sequencing sections on a landing page for problem-aware visitors such as Facebook ad traffic.
steps: Call out the exact pain point so the visitor thinks 'this is exactly me.'
Agitate the problem — turn up the heat and describe what they have already tried and failed at.
Present your solution as a clear way out, with a compelling reason to act and a CTA button right there.
Position this section directly beneath the above-the-fold area if your audience is problem-aware but does not yet know the solution (the source did this for a coaching client).
For more solution-aware audiences (the source's laser eye surgery client), move this section further down, after social proof, and make it shorter — less education and trust-building copy is needed.
caveats: Section length should match awareness level; the source itself varies placement by audience rather than applying one fixed order.

cards.title: Reuse One Section Template Across Niches
cards.summary: The same section principles (e.g., pain-agitate-solution, social proof) recur in different designs across clients.
cards.use_when: Adapting proven landing page sections to a new niche or brand without reinventing layout.
steps: Identify the underlying principle for each section (e.g., alternate social proof with value propositions).
Change only the visual design — graphics, layout, brand colors — to fit the client or audience, keeping the principle intact.
The same template was used for clients with very different niches, from SaaS, e-commerce, coaching, to HVAC, beauty/cosmetics, and medical, only the content and styling changed.
Apply this to your own store by keeping a library of section templates you restyle per product line or campaign rather than writing each landing page from zero.
caveats: The source stresses no two landing pages are identical; templates are a starting point, not a copy-paste substitute for research.

cards.title: Build Value Props from Benefit, Not Feature
cards.summary: Convert each product or service feature into a benefit statement that answers 'so that...'
cards.use_when: Writing value prop sections, PDP bullets, or bundle descriptions.
steps: List every selling point of the business or product. The source lists things like data-driven decisions, 400+ landing pages of experience, in-house copywriters, boutique team size, and a detailed strategy process.
For each selling point, ask 'so that...' to translate the feature into what the customer gets. Example: 'clear and timely reports' (feature) becomes 'make smarter and faster decisions' (benefit).
Write the actual benefit into the headline of that value prop section.
Aim for three to four value prop sections as a bare minimum, and eight to ten for more complex offers.
The source reports scattering social proof between value prop sections contributed to a 187% lift in qualified leads and conversions for one client.
caveats: The 187% figure is a specific client example with multiple simultaneous changes, so the value prop change cannot be isolated as the sole cause.

cards.title: Generate Value Prop Headlines at Scale
cards.summary: List selling points in a design canvas, then write headline variants for each.
cards.use_when: Rapidly producing value prop headline variants for a page build or redesign.
steps: Open your design tool (the source uses Figma) and list all selling points of the business on the side.
Write a benefit-driven headline for each selling point, using a repeatable headline framework rather than ad-hoc brainstorming.
Plug the resulting headlines into the value prop sections further down the page.
Keep every headline benefit-first. The source refuses generic headlines like 'our services,' 'here's what we do,' or 'what makes us unique.'
caveats: Headline frameworks need to be your own; the source's framework is proprietary and not included here.

cards.title: Write Headlines for Scanners, Not Readers
cards.summary: Assume visitors only read headlines, and put the benefit in every headline.
cards.use_when: Writing any headline, section title, value prop heading, or review summary on a landing page or PDP.
steps: Operate on the source's premise that people read only about 20% of page content and scan the rest.
Write each headline so it works standalone — assume body text is never read. The source's rule: the actual benefit goes in the headline.
Avoid generic section headers like 'our services' or 'here's what we do.'
Apply this to social proof too: put a headline above testimonials that summarizes the review at a high level, so a scanner still gets the benefit.
caveats: The 20% reading figure is a general content-consumption rule of thumb — use it to justify headline discipline rather than as a precise measurement of your own traffic.

cards.title: Build a Wall of Love Social Proof Section
cards.summary: Combine video and text reviews with source attribution and headline summaries to create verifiable, scannable social proof.
cards.use_when: Designing a social proof section for a landing page, PDP, or services page.
steps: Mix video reviews and text reviews in one section so visitors consume a large volume of proof.
Put the source of each review in the bottom-right corner (e.g., Google, Trustpilot) so reviews are verifiable and credibility is higher.
Write a headline above each review that encapsulates the review's point at a high level, so people scanning headlines still get the strongest claim.
On mobile, lay everything out in the open — do not hide it in a carousel. The source says carousels statistically have very low engagement rates.
Repeat social proof in multiple sections throughout the page rather than once, treating the page as a journey where each uncertainty point gets another proof point.
caveats: Review-source attribution should reflect real, verifiable reviews. Carousel performance may differ on your site; the source treats the low-engagement claim as a general pattern.

cards.title: Rotate Case Studies and Creative Social Proof Formats
cards.summary: Vary social proof formats across the page to keep serving proof at every critical juncture.
cards.use_when: Deciding how many social proof formats to include and where to place them on a long page.
steps: Use logos or a scrolling logo strip early, then case studies further down. The source did both for one client.
For an HVAC client, combine a rotating carousel that shows an actual installation image with a review underneath — one section completing two jobs (visual proof and testimonial).
For SaaS or digital products, pair video testimonials with stats of client results the product produced.
Place proof between critical value prop sections to signal that clients — not just the company — are saying it.
caveats: If you follow the source's anti-carousel advice elsewhere, distinguish content carousels (avoid) from a rotating installation-plus-review format (used successfully).

cards.title: Place Social Proof Before or After Pain Section by Awareness
cards.summary: Move social proof above the pain section when buyers are solution-aware and ready to buy.
cards.use_when: Ordering sections on a landing page for high-intent traffic.
steps: Default order after the above-the-fold section is pain-agitate-solution, with social proof appearing after value props.

For high-intent, solution-aware users ready to buy, swap the pain section and the social proof section, moving social proof up so it leads directly under the above the fold, and placing the pain point section underneath it.

For the source's laser eye surgery client, who serves a solution-aware audience, place the pain section much further down, after the social proof, and keep it shorter because less education is needed.
Match section depth to audience: problem-aware traffic needs long, direct-response copy; solution-aware traffic needs less copy and less trust-building.
caveats: The source presents these as layouts that depend on traffic source and awareness, not a single universal order to apply to all pages.

cards.title: Design Social Proof for Scanners
cards.summary: Make each review readable at a glance with a summary headline and a visible source label.
cards.use_when: Reformatting testimonials or review blocks for a landing page or PDP where scanning dominates.
steps: Write a headline that captures the review's core claim, e.g. 'my vision improved to 20/12' or 'I feel better knowing I'm covered for the next 10 years.'
Assume no one reads the body text; the headline alone must give a compelling reason to act.
Label the source visibly, e.g. Google or Trustpilot, so people know the review can be verified.
Lay out reviews openly on mobile rather than tucking them into a carousel.
Vary the format (text rows, video tiles, stat callouts, rotating image-plus-review) while keeping the scannable structure consistent.
caveats: Attribution and quotes should be accurate; do not fabricate review sources or claims.

cards.title: Comparison Table for Complex Offers
cards.summary: Show differences against alternatives in a scannable table with check and X marks, adding explanatory lines only where needed.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a product against competing options or traditional alternatives on a landing page.
steps: Build a table comparing the brand to alternatives. One source example compares a procedure against traditional procedures and against glasses and contacts.
Use X's and check marks so the differences are scannable and digestible rather than prose.
For more complex offers requiring context, add a line of explanatory text inside the table to help the visitor understand each difference.
Treat the table as a benefit-driven section — it still needs to make the case, not just list attributes.
caveats: Comparison claims should be factual and defensible; avoid stacking the table with unsupportable attributes.

cards.title: How It Works Section with a Benefit Final Step
cards.summary: Explain the process in three or four steps and always end on the promised outcome.
cards.use_when: Writing the how-it-works section of a landing page or product page.
steps: Lay out the steps at a high level so the visitor sees the process clearly.
Make the perceived likelihood of success high and the effort feel low — the source stresses making the process feel effortless in three or four steps.

End the sequence with the end benefit, not just the last mechanical step. Example: step 1 fill out the form, step 2 watch the free webinar, step 3 talk to a specialist, step 4 start feeling better in under 12 weeks.
For an ecommerce store, translate process steps into something like order, receive bundle, follow the routine, and end on the outcome the product delivers.
caveats: Do not invent steps or timelines your operations cannot actually support; keep the final outcome claim honest.

cards.title: Section Order for a Complete Landing Page
cards.summary: Sequence core sections so education, proof, value, process, team, guarantee, FAQ, and closer each do their job.
cards.use_when: Planning the full structure of a new landing page or auditing a poorly converting one.
steps: Start with the above-the-fold section (headline, body, stats, form, social proof, phone, CTA as applicable).
Place a second social proof section after value props, and rotate in more social proof at each critical juncture.
Add a benefit-driven headline section with three to six further selling points, which can be designed as cards, a comparison table, or a stats layout depending on the brand.
Follow with a how-it-works section, then meet the team for service-based, B2B, clinic, or trades businesses (people buy from people).
Add an optional guarantee section — the source says this is optional and can be replaced with a social proof or value prop section if no guarantee exists.

Close with one more social proof section, FAQs drawn from common sales call questions, and a closer section with a benefit-driven headline, subheadline, two forms of social proof, three to five expectation bullets, and a simplified form.
caveats: This order is the source's recommended layout for service and B2B lead pages; the source explicitly varies order by awareness and offer type.

cards.title: Build a Closer Section with Benefit Recap and Trust
cards.summary: Replace generic contact-section copy with a full recapped pitch plus form and trust elements.
cards.use_when: Designing the final conversion section of a B2B or service landing page.
steps: Do not use generic headlines like 'contact us' or 'get a quote' — the visitor already knows they are at the contact section.
Write one large benefit-driven headline recapping the dream outcome the visitor cares about.
Add a subheadline giving one final reason to get in touch.
Include two forms of social proof, matching the above-the-fold section.
Add three to five bullets of what people can expect if they fill out the form, giving a clear incentive.
Keep the form simple: combine first and last name into full name unless there is a specific reason to split them, and separate labels from placeholders.
caveats: The source's advice is aimed at lead gen and service-based pages; ecommerce closers use product selection and cart mechanics instead.

cards.title: Value Stack for Courses and Educational Offers
cards.summary: Structure a course or certificate closer as stacked modules each paired with proof.
cards.use_when: Selling a course, program, certificate, or educational offer on a landing page.
steps: Open with an overview of everything included: number of videos, hours of content, and perks.
Stack value module by module, for each module stating what the buyer gets.
Follow each module with a testimonial that complements it.
Continue the module-plus-testimonial pattern to make the buyer feel they are getting their money's worth.
Use this structure instead of the standard lead-gen closer when selling education rather than a service call.
caveats: Only use proof that is genuine and matched to the module; do not fabricate testimonials.

cards.title: Ecommerce Product Selection and Add-to-Cart Flow
cards.summary: Make product selection seamless, show bundle savings, and avoid disruptive cart refreshes.
cards.use_when: Designing the product selection, bundle, and add-to-cart experience on an ecommerce page.
steps: Place product selection toward the top of the page, since it is the main action for ecommerce.
If multiple bundles exist, show exactly what the customer saves. The source states you should not make people do math, and says they have A/B tested this repeatedly.
Put social proof and risk reduction near the point of action to get people over the edge.
Avoid full-page refreshes just to confirm an add-to-cart. The source calls this extremely disruptive and says it will hurt conversion rate.
Use a sliding cart menu that slides out on add-to-cart, so you can cross-sell and upsell inside the cart, improving both conversion rate and AOV.
caveats: The source's conversion claims for these patterns are their own tested observations, not universal guarantees.
